strengths: The proposed iterative paradigm is a clean and well-motivated alternative to auto-regressive and reference-image paradigms for long story visualization, directly addressing error accumulation and reference-flaw propagation.

Global Reference Cross-Attention (GRCA) is an elegant training-free design: reusing pre-trained IP-Adapter cross-attention weights with low-dimensional CLIP global embeddings keeps the method plug-and-play and scalable to many reference images (validated in Fig. 8).

Comprehensive experimental coverage: regular-length benchmark (StorySalon), self-curated long stories (up to 100 frames), subject-consistent generation comparison, computational cost analysis, extensive ablations (initialization, GRCA vs. CSA, weighting strategy, number of iterations), and human evaluation.

Quantitative results are competitive: improvements in aCCS and aFID over StoryDiffusion and StoryGen on both regular-length and long-story settings, with supporting qualitative results across many figures.

Thorough appendix, including the trade-off between iterations and CLIP-T (Tab. 6), which honestly documents the consistency/alignment trade-off of the iterative scheme; code and project page are promised for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core mechanism is essentially applying IP-Adapter (off-the-shelf weights) iteratively with a linearly scheduled weighting factor; no new training or learned components are introduced, and the linear weighting schedule appears to be a heuristic tuned on limited cases.

Computational cost is understated: while per-image FLOPs w.r.t. the number of references are reported, the full pipeline runs L=10 full 50-step diffusion passes over all B frames, i.e., roughly 10x the compute of a single-pass baseline; an end-to-end wall-clock/total-FLOPs comparison with StoryDiffusion and IP-Adapter for a complete story is missing.

Long-story evaluation is self-curated: stories are generated by GPT-4o with no ground-truth images, making the meaning of aFID unclear (computed between what distributions?), and CLIP-based metrics are known to be weak proxies for character consistency and interaction correctness; claims about 'fine-grained interactions' rest largely on cherry-picked qualitative examples.

Some experimental inconsistencies raise concerns: in Tab. 3 the 'GRCA' row exactly duplicates the 'w/o Iteration Paradigm' row, and the ablation of the iteration paradigm is not fully isolated (initialization vs. iteration vs. weighting contributions are entangled); human evaluation lacks details on number of raters, agreement, and statistical significance.

Within an iteration, frames are generated independently from the previous iteration only, so no within-iteration coherence mechanism exists; the paper does not analyze failure modes such as identity drift toward the 'average' of references or degradation of rare/emerging characters over many iterations beyond a couple of anecdotes.
The linear weighting strategy (λ from 0.3 to 0.5) and the choice of 10 iterations are validated only on a small set of GPT-4o-generated stories; sensitivity analysis across datasets/styles is thin.

strengths: The proposed iterative paradigm for long story visualization (up to 100 frames) is a reasonable and practical idea, and framing it against the Auto-Regressive and Reference-Image paradigms is a clear way to position the contribution.

GRCA operates on low-dimensional CLIP global embeddings rather than intermediate denoising features, and the computational cost comparison (Fig. 8) supports the claimed scalability advantage over CSA.

The evaluation covers regular-length (StorySalon) and long story settings, includes human evaluation, subject-consistent generation comparisons, and ablations over the iterative paradigm, initialization, and GRCA vs. CSA.
The method is training-free and plug-and-play, which improves reproducibility and ease of adoption, and code is stated to be released.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially IP-Adapter-style reference cross-attention applied iteratively over CLIP global embeddings, with a linear weighting schedule. The core components (CLIP embeddings as keys/values, reuse of pretrained cross-attention weights) are largely inherited from IP-Adapter, and the conceptual contribution of 'iterate over previous outputs' is a straightforward wrapper rather than a new modeling insight.

The results are not convincing: in Table 1, the base Story-Adapter (CLIP-T 0.305, aCCS 0.760, aFID 16.52) actually loses to StoryDiffusion (0.311/0.765/14.84), and only the SDXL-based variant wins. In Table 2, IP-AdapterXL achieves a lower aFID (88.69) than Story-AdapterXL (94.30). The headline gains come primarily from swapping in a stronger backbone (SDXL), not from the proposed method itself — a confound that undermines the central claims.

Iterating 10 times multiplies inference cost by roughly 10x, which directly contradicts the paper's emphasis on 'computational efficiency'. The claimed efficiency of GRCA is only relative to CSA per image, while the overall pipeline cost versus baselines is never reported.

Potential unfairness in evaluation: 'Prompt-SDM' uses 'cartoon-style images' prompts while other methods receive full story prompts; long-story benchmarks are self-curated with GPT-4o and not standardized; some entries in Table 2 seem inconsistent with the implementation description (e.g., 'unclassified classifier guidance' is contradictory).

Ablation numbers are internally inconsistent and confusing: Table 3 lists 'w/o Iteration Paradigm' (0.322/0.757/105.17) identically to 'GRCA' and to the 1st-iteration row in Table 6, and 'Ours' (0.318 aCCS-wise CLIP-T 0.318) is worse than 'w/o Iteration Paradigm' (0.322) on CLIP-T, which needs explanation. Also 'Iteration Paradigm, λ=0.5' shows aFID 81.72 — better than the final model — yet is described as 'excessive consistency', without reconciliation.

The linear weighting strategy (λ from 0.3 to 0.5) is ad hoc with no theoretical or empirical justification for why linear interpolation or these endpoints are optimal; the ablation of the schedule is thin.

Long-story error-accumulation claims are supported mostly by anecdotal qualitative figures; the long story evaluation set (20 GPT-4o-generated stories) is too small and non-standard to substantiate the claims of superiority over error accumulation.

Writing and presentation issues: ambiguous statements ('unclassified classifier guidance'), repetitive paradigm discussion (main text vs. Appendix A), and figures that are hard to verify at reduced resolution weaken the clarity.

strengths: The iterative paradigm is a reasonable and clearly articulated alternative to auto-regressive and reference-image paradigms for story visualization, and the paper is well-motivated with a good taxonomy of existing approaches.

GRCA is elegant in reusing pre-trained IP-Adapter cross-attention weights without training, and the global CLIP embeddings keep memory/compute per image nearly constant with story length (Fig. 8), addressing a genuine scalability limitation of CSA-based methods.

Evaluation is fairly comprehensive for this line of work: regular-length benchmark (StorySalon), a self-curated long-story setting (up to 100 frames), subject-consistent generation comparison, human evaluation across three tasks, ablations of each component, and an iteration-count study.
The ablation (Tab. 3) and iteration study (Tab. 6) are transparent enough to reveal the trade-offs (e.g., CLIP-T degradation with more iterations), which increases trust in the reported results.
Code release is promised, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core technical component (GRCA) is essentially IP-Adapter's decoupled cross-attention applied iteratively with CLIP global embeddings, reusing pre-trained weights unchanged. The main contribution is a system-level recipe (initialization + iteration + linear weighting schedule) rather than a new method, and the linear weighting strategy is heuristic with no analysis justifying the schedule.

The claimed 'computationally efficient' framing is misleading: per-image FLOPs are constant (Fig. 8), but the full pipeline runs 10 iterations × 50 DDIM steps over all B frames, i.e., roughly 10× the total inference cost of a single pass. No end-to-end wall-clock or total-cost comparison against StoryDiffusion or IP-Adapter is provided.

The consistency gains may partly reflect convergence toward a mode/mean appearance rather than genuine semantic consistency: CLIP-T drops substantially as iterations increase (0.330 → 0.297 at 15 iterations; also 0.322 → 0.261 with fixed λ=0.5), and the paper does not analyze or mitigate this diversity/text-faithfulness collapse (e.g., no seed control, no analysis of within-story variation).

Benchmark concerns: the long-story evaluation uses only 20 GPT-4o-curated stories with self-defined protocols; aFID on non-comparable, stylistically dissimilar generated sets is of dubious validity, and mixed quantitative results are under-discussed (e.g., base Story-Adapter loses to StoryDiffusion on aFID/aCCS in Tab. 1, and IP-Adapter has lower aFID in Tab. 2).

Tab. 3 is confusing: the 'GRCA' row duplicates the 'w/o Iteration Paradigm' row exactly, and the GRCA-vs-CSA comparison conflates the attention mechanism with the iteration count, making the design-choice attribution unclear.
Missing comparisons to recent related methods cited in the paper (e.g., StoryImager, Shen et al. 2024), which weakens the SoTA claim.

Writing/clarity issues remain: some notation in Eqs. (1) and (3) is sloppy (e.g., index ranges, reused symbols c_{1,..,B} across projections), and the text repeats marketing-style claims ('fine-grained interactions') without a precise metric for interaction quality.

strengths: The paper identifies a real and well-motivated problem: existing auto-regressive and reference-image paradigms both degrade on long story visualization, and the proposed external iterative paradigm (reusing all frames from the previous round as references) is a sensible, conceptually clean solution.

GRCA is training-free and plug-and-play, and the use of compact global CLIP embeddings (rather than intermediate denoising features) makes referencing 100+ frames computationally feasible, as demonstrated in the scalability analysis (Fig. 13, Tab. 6).

Evaluation is broad: regular-length (StorySalon) and long-story settings, comparisons against many baselines including recent ones (ConsiStory, 1prompt1story, FLUX.1-Kontext, Nano Banana), human evaluation, ablations of GRCA settings (sliding window, random set, mean-pooling), weighting strategy, iteration count, and efficiency/variants (Story-Iter-Fast, ControlNet integration).

The paper is transparent about limitations (consistency–diversity trade-off, CLIP-T degradation with more iterations, inference cost) and offers honest ablation reporting, e.g., showing 'w/o Initialization' achieves better aFID.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited. GRCA is essentially IP-Adapter's decoupled cross-attention applied to a concatenation of CLIP global embeddings from the previous round, and the 'iterative paradigm' reduces to repeatedly re-running the model with its own outputs. The core machinery is a fairly straightforward composition of existing components (CLIP + IP-Adapter weights + repeated sampling) with a linearly scheduled weighting factor.

Ablation evidence for the full method is mixed and partially undermines the central claims: in Tab. 4 the full model has lower CLIP-T than both 'w/o GRCA' and 'w/o Iteration Paradigm', and higher aFID than 'w/o Initialization'; in Tab. 6, CSA beats GRCA on all three quality metrics in the first iteration, so GRCA's advantage rests mainly on qualitative examples and scalability rather than on quantitative gains.

The proposed long-story benchmark is weak: only 20 GPT-4o-generated stories (10 x 50-sentence, 10 x 100-sentence), with no ground-truth images, making aFID/aCCS/CLIP-T comparisons on synthetic prompts an unreliable proxy for true long-narrative quality. Metric definitions (aFID between reference crops and later crops of detected objects via Grounding-DINO) introduce detection-noise sensitivity that the paper asserts but does not thoroughly validate.

Quantitative improvements are modest. On the regular-length benchmark, Story-IterXL gains over StoryDiffusion are small (aFID 14.63 vs 14.84) and the headline claims of 'state-of-the-art' rely heavily on the weaker long-story setting.

Computational cost is a practical concern: 250 minutes for a 100-frame story at 10 iterations (Tab. 3/9). The Fast variant regresses notably on quality (aFID 109 vs 94), so the efficiency-quality trade-off is not fully resolved.

Presentation issues: duplicated 'Story-Iter' row in the long-story panel of Tab. 8 (apparently Story-IterXL), missing details on human evaluation protocol (number of raters, statistical significance), and some over-claiming in the abstract/intro relative to the mixed ablation results.

Diversity is likely under-measured given a single fixed random seed for all experiments; the acknowledged consistency–diversity trade-off deserves quantitative diversity metrics beyond a brief appendix mention.

strengths: The paper is well-organized and easy to follow, with a clearly articulated motivation that fixed-reference (RI) and auto-regressive (AR) paradigms fail on long stories.
The method is training-free and plug-and-play, reusing IP-Adapter weights, which makes the approach broadly applicable and reproducible.

The evaluation is extensive: regular-length (StorySalon) and long-story settings, multiple baselines including recent editing models (FLUX.1.Kontext, Nano Banana), human evaluation, efficiency analysis (Tab. 3/9), and multiple ablations (GRCA settings, weighting strategy, initialization, iteration count).

The computational analysis (Tab. 6, Fig. 13) convincingly shows GRCA's global embeddings scale better than StoryDiffusion's CSA for many reference frames, which is the strongest technical justification for the design.
The new long-story benchmark (up to 100 frames) addresses a real gap, since existing benchmarks top out at much shorter sequences.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The core idea is essentially: (a) IP-Adapter-style global-embedding cross-attention applied to multiple reference frames, and (b) feeding the previous round's outputs back as references for several refinement rounds. Both are straightforward engineering choices, and the paper does not provide any theoretical analysis of convergence or guarantees that this self-referential refinement converges to a good fixed point rather than degenerating.

The empirical gains are modest and inconsistent. In Tab. 1, the non-XL Story-Iter is worse than StoryDiffusion on CLIP-T and aCCS (0.305/0.760 vs 0.311/0.765), and in Tab. 4 the 'w/o Initialization' ablation achieves a better aFID (90.30) than the full method (94.30). In Tab. 6, GRCA actually loses to CSA on aCCS and aFID; the argument for GRCA rests purely on scalability. The headline claims of 'state-of-the-art' are thus weaker than the tables suggest.

CLIP-T consistently degrades as iterations increase (0.330 at initialization to 0.297 at iteration 15 in Tab. 11), revealing a fundamental consistency-vs-alignment trade-off that is acknowledged but not resolved; the chosen default (10 iterations, λ∈[0.3,0.5]) is ad hoc, and Tab. 5 shows [0.3,0.6] yields better aCCS/aFID than the selected configuration, suggesting hand-tuning on test data.

The long-story benchmark is very thin: only 20 GPT-4o-generated stories (10×50 and 10×100 sentences), with no ground-truth images, making aFID/aCCS computed purely among self-generated outputs and raising concerns about circularity of the evaluation protocol.

Efficiency remains a practical weakness: 250 minutes for a 100-frame story at 1024 resolution, and the Fast variant recovers speed only by sacrificing aFID (109.13 vs 94.30), partially undermining the practical value of the paradigm.

Several presentation errors undermine confidence: Tab. 8 lists 'Story-Iter' twice in the long-story section (presumably a mislabeled Story-IterXL row), Tab. 9 refers to an undefined 'Story-IterL', and Table 11's aFID header is marked '↑' while lower is better. The 'Nano Banana' baseline lacks a proper citation.

The iterative paradigm risks mode collapse / homogenization of the story (referencing all previous frames pulls every frame toward the average appearance), which the paper admits in the limitations but only addresses with future-work plans; the diversity analysis (Sec. H.3) is qualitative rather than quantitative.

Comparisons with editing models (Sec. D) partially conflate task mismatch with method superiority—editing models are designed to preserve reference identity, so their lower CLIP-T on this benchmark is expected and does not directly validate Story-Iter's design.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and increasingly important problem: maintaining semantic consistency and character interactions in long (up to 100 frames) story visualization, where existing AR and reference-image paradigms degrade.

The proposed external iterative paradigm is a sensible reframing: using all frames from the previous external iteration as references, with CLIP global embeddings, avoids the memory blow-up of self-attention over intermediate denoising features (CSA) and avoids error propagation of fixed references, and this is supported by the GRCA vs. CSA comparison (Tab. 6, Fig. 13) and the GRCA setting ablations (Tab. 7).

The method is training-free and plug-and-play (reusing IP-Adapter weights), which makes it practical and reproducible; pseudocode, implementation details, and code in supplementary material are provided.

The evaluation is quite comprehensive: regular-length (StorySalon) and long-story settings, many baselines including very recent systems (StoryDiffusion, ConsiStory, 1prompt1story, FLUX.1.Kontext, Nano Banana), human evaluation, ablations of initialization/GRCA/weighting strategy, efficiency analysis, and useful variants (Story-Iter-Fast with LCM, Story-Iter-ControlNet).

The paper is honest about limitations: the consistency vs. text-alignment trade-off across iterations (Tab. 11 shows CLIP-T dropping from 0.330 to 0.297) and the efficiency cost of 10 external iterations are discussed, with a fast variant proposed.
The new 100-frame long-story benchmark addresses a gap, since existing benchmarks cover at most ~44 frames.
weaknesses: The core novelty is modest: the method essentially wraps IP-Adapter-style decoupled cross-attention in an outer re-generation loop over the full story. The GRCA module is a straightforward projection of CLIP global embeddings into keys/values, and the linear weighting scheme is simple; the contribution is more an engineering combination than a fundamentally new technique.

The long-story benchmark is small and self-curated: only 20 GPT-4o-generated narratives (10 x 50-sentence, 10 x 100-sentence). Evaluation on 20 stories with metrics like aFID computed over crops may be noisy, and the benchmark construction could favor the proposed method. The claimed new benchmark contribution is therefore thin without public release details or more stories.

Some quantitative results are mixed rather than clearly winning: on regular-length stories, Story-IterXL has lower CLIP-T (0.310) than StoryDiffusion (0.311) and the aFID gap over IP-AdapterXL (14.70 vs 14.63) is negligible; in Tab. 4 the 'w/o initialization' ablation actually achieves the best aFID (90.30), and in Tab. 6 GRCA is worse than CSA in both aCCS and aFID at the first iteration. The narrative of consistent SOTA is somewhat stronger than the numbers.

The consistency-alignment trade-off means the method needs careful hyperparameter tuning (number of iterations, lambda schedule) per story; results in Tab. 5 suggest sensitivity to the weighting schedule, which weakens the plug-and-play claim.

Computational cost is significant: 250 minutes and 43 PFLOPs for 100 frames with Story-IterXL. The Fast variant (20 min) degrades quality notably (aCCS 0.788 vs 0.802, aFID 109 vs 94), so the practical Pareto point is not clearly established.

Several presentation issues undermine polish: Tab. 8's long-story table lists 'Story-Iter' twice (the second is presumably Story-IterXL), Tab. 11's aFID column is marked with an upward arrow although it should be downward, and Table 2 mixes non-comparable systems (closed-source Nano Banana, DALL·E 3) whose generation setups differ, complicating fairness of comparison.
Fixed random seed and default 10 iterations used in all main experiments raises questions about seed robustness; no variance reporting or multiple-seed experiments are provided.
